:::{#exm-risk-epi}
#### One-year risk of influenza

Suppose we follow 2000 people for one year,
nobody is lost to follow-up,
and 30 of them develop influenza during that year.
The estimated one-year risk of influenza in this population is
the proportion who developed influenza:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\pi
&= \frac{\text{number who developed influenza}}{\text{number followed}}
&& \text{(sample proportion estimates the probability)}\\
&= \frac{30}{2000}
&& \text{(substitute the counts)}\\
&= 0.015
&& \text{(divide)}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-risk-epi-counterexample}
#### A case count is not a risk

The count of 30 influenza cases from @exm-risk-epi is not a risk:
it is not a probability,
and it does not account for how many people were at risk.
If instead 4000 people had been followed for the same year,
with the same 30 cases,
the estimated risk would be:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\pi
&= \frac{30}{4000}
&& \text{(substitute the counts)}\\
&= 0.0075
&& \text{(divide)}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is half the risk from @exm-risk-epi,
even though the case count is identical.
:::
